answer.label: Not Thomas Jefferson — a modern spurious quotation
answer.authorDates: 1743–1826 · 3rd U.S. President & principal author of the Declaration of Independence
answer.sourceLine: This line appears in none of Jefferson’s writings or recorded speeches. The Thomas Jefferson Foundation flags it as spurious, its earliest documented attribution to him being a 2002 newspaper letter — three books then spread it widely in 2004 — and it runs against Jefferson’s own faith in majority rule and self-government.

source.excerpt: A democracy is nothing more than mob rule, where fifty-one percent of the people may take away the rights of the other forty-nine.
trail: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation lists this among its spurious quotations, stating it has “no evidence to confirm that Thomas Jefferson ever said or wrote” it.

Snopes finds the variants “became widely attributed to Jefferson only since… three books of 2004.” Monticello’s own encyclopedia record dates the earliest documented occurrence earlier — a 28 September 2002 letter to the Tampa Tribune.
Check Your Fact rates the attribution false, dating the misattribution to at least 2002 via etymologist Barry Popik.
Etymologist Barry Popik traces “democracy is mob rule” phrasing back through the 20th century (e.g. 1888, 1929) with no link to the Founders.
source.excerptNote: No primary source — letter, speech, book, or diary — has ever been produced for this wording. It is presented here as the circulating text, not as anything Jefferson wrote.

author.name: Thomas Jefferson
author.heading: Why the words don’t fit the man
author.metaLine: 1743–1826 · 3rd U.S. President & author of the Declaration of Independence
author.bio: Jefferson was a lifelong champion of majority rule and the capacity of ordinary people to govern themselves — he wrote of his faith in “the will of the majority” as the natural law of any just society. A blanket condemnation of democracy as “mob rule” sits against his documented convictions, which is one reason his own foundation flags this line as spurious. The sentiment it expresses belongs to a much older strain of anti-democratic criticism, not to Jefferson.

copyAttribution: Misattributed to Thomas Jefferson. The Thomas Jefferson Foundation (Monticello) lists this "mob rule / 51 percent" line as a spurious quotation with no source in Jefferson's writings; it appears in print only from the 2000s.

misattribution.heading: How a modern slogan got a Founding Father’s name
misattribution.intro: This is a classic magnet misattribution: a punchy anti-democracy slogan pinned on Jefferson to borrow his authority, despite contradicting what he actually believed.

items.why: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation states it has “no evidence to confirm that Thomas Jefferson ever said or wrote” this line or its variants, and finds it attributed to him only from books published around 2004. See the Monticello record.
Criticism of pure democracy as “mob rule” long predates any Founder — Barry Popik documents the phrasing in print in 1888 and 1929, well before it was reframed as a Jefferson quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: No primary source exists: the “51 percent / 49 percent” wording is a modern coinage falsely draped on Jefferson, as the fact-checks and his own estate confirm.

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: The line thrives because it is quotable and ideologically useful: it compresses a real debate — how a majority can threaten minority rights — into a single barbed sentence, and Jefferson’s name lends it instant gravity. That the sentiment cuts against his actual views is precisely what makes the attribution seductive and misleading.

Monticello’s researchers note that “mob rule” criticism of democracy runs through 20th-century print but only hardened into a Founding Father attribution late in the century, with the Jefferson version surfacing in books around 2004.
context.pull: A punchy slogan borrowing a Founder’s authority — against everything that Founder actually argued.
